flavors.text: You knew every bolt and gasket, but the books never added up. The lot went quiet one Tuesday, and it stayed that way.
You structured deals for Fortune 500s. In the end, your own ledger was the one that buried you.
Your father built this from nothing. You returned it to nothing.
They said you knew what was wrong before you sold it. The AG's office agreed.
Regulatory proceedings. The kind you used to advise clients to settle fast. You didn't.
The regulars who remembered your father remember something else now.
Twenty years in the shop, and it ends in a courtroom. The DA had the VINs memorized.
Wire fraud. The irony was not lost on anyone, least of all your former employer.
The family name made the headline. Your father would have understood — it was in the blood.
You closed the bay door for the last time. The wrenches went to your nephew. The cash went to a cabin upstate.
A second retirement, this one earned slower and felt sweeter. The numbers, for once, were yours alone.
Your father retired into a bottle. You retired into a quiet boat. The name on the door comes down Friday.
The PE folks wired the money before the ink dried. You don't recognize the new signage. You don't drive past.
You knew the playbook from the other side of the table. The buyer paid full freight and called it a steal.
The family name comes off the marquee Monday. The check is enough that you stopped reading the news about it.
You handed your kid the keys with a callused palm. They'll do it differently. That's the point.
Two generations now. The legacy you never had at the bank, built brick by brick on a paved lot.
Three generations. Your father would have called it a miracle. You call it a Tuesday.
